1	# Introduction to Tabular
2	
3	Polished terminal output requires two things: good formatting (see [Rendering Introduction](intro-to-rendering.md)) and good layouts. For text-only, non-interactive output, layout mostly means aligning things vertically and controlling how multiple pieces of information are presented together.
4	
5	Tabular provides a declarative column system with powerful primitives for sizing (fixed, range, fill, fractions), positioning (anchor to right), overflow handling (clip, wrap, truncate), cell alignment, and automated per-column styling.
6	
7	Tabular is not only about tables. Any listing where items have multiple fields that benefit from vertical alignment is a good candidate—log entries with authors, timestamps, and messages; file listings with names, sizes, and dates; task lists with IDs, titles, and statuses. Add headers, separators, and borders to a tabular layout, and you have a table.
8	
9	**Key capabilities:**
10	
11	- **Flexible sizing**: Fixed widths, min/max ranges, fill remaining space, fractional proportions
12	- **Smart truncation**: Truncate at start, middle, or end with custom ellipsis
13	- **Word wrapping**: Wrap long content across multiple lines with proper alignment
14	- **Unicode-aware**: CJK characters, combining marks, and ANSI codes handled correctly
15	- **Dynamic styling**: Style columns or individual values based on content
16	
17	In this guide, we will walk from a simple listing to a polished table, exploring the available features.
18	
19	**See Also:**
20	
21	- [Introduction to Rendering](intro-to-rendering.md) - templates and styles overview
22	- [Styling System](../topics/styling-system.md) - themes and adaptive styles
23	
24	---
25	
26	## Our Example: Task List
27	
28	We'll build the output for a task list. This is a perfect Tabular use case: each task has an index, title, and status. We want them aligned, readable, and visually clear at a glance.
29	
30	Here's our data:
31	
32	```rust
33	use serde::Serialize;
34	
35	#[derive(Clone, Serialize)]
36	#[serde(rename_all = "lowercase")]
37	pub enum Status { Pending, Done }
38	
39	#[derive(Clone, Serialize)]
40	struct Task {
41	    title: String,
42	    status: Status,
43	}
44	
45	let tasks = vec![
46	    Task { title: "Implement user authentication".into(), status: Status::Pending },
47	    Task { title: "Fix payment gateway timeout".into(), status: Status::Pending },
48	    Task { title: "Update documentation for API v2".into(), status: Status::Done },
49	    Task { title: "Review pull request #142".into(), status: Status::Pending },
50	];
51	```
52	
53	Let's progressively build this from raw output to a polished, professional listing.
54	
55	---
56	
57	## Step 1: The Problem with Plain Output
58	
59	Without any formatting, a naive approach might look like this:
60	
61	```jinja
62	{% for task in tasks %}
63	{{ loop.index }}. {{ task.title }} {{ task.status }}
64	{% endfor %}
65	```
66	
67	Output:
68	
69	```text
70	1. Implement user authentication pending
71	2. Fix payment gateway timeout pending
72	3. Update documentation for API v2 done
73	4. Review pull request #142 pending
74	```
75	
76	This is barely readable. Fields run together, nothing aligns, and scanning the list requires mental parsing of each line. Let's fix that.
77	
78	---
79	
80	## Step 2: Basic Column Alignment with `col`
81	
82	The simplest improvement is the `col` filter. It pads (or truncates) each value to a fixed width:
83	
84	```jinja
85	{% for task in tasks %}
86	{{ loop.index | col(4) }}  {{ task.status | col(10) }}  {{ task.title | col(40) }}
87	{% endfor %}
88	```
89	
90	Output:
91	
92	```text
93	1.    pending     Implement user authentication
94	2.    pending     Fix payment gateway timeout
95	3.    done        Update documentation for API v2
96	4.    pending     Review pull request #142
97	```
98	
99	Already much better. Each column aligns vertically, making it easy to scan. But we've hardcoded widths, and if a title is too long, it gets truncated with `...`.
100	
101	> **Key insight:** The `col` filter handles Unicode correctly. CJK characters count as 2 columns, combining marks don't add width, and ANSI escape codes are preserved but not counted.
102	
103	---
104	
105	## Step 3: Structured Layout with `tabular()`
106	
107	For more control, use the `tabular()` function. This creates a formatter that you configure once and use for all rows:
108	
109	```jinja
110	{% set t = tabular([
111	    {"name": "index", "width": 4},
112	    {"name": "status", "width": 10},
113	    {"name": "title", "width": 40}
114	], separator="  ") %}
115	
116	{% for task in tasks %}
117	{{ t.row([loop.index, task.status, task.title]) }}
118	{% endfor %}
119	```
120	
121	The output looks the same, but now the column definitions are centralized. This becomes powerful when we start adding features.
122	
123	---
124	
125	## Step 4: Flexible Widths
126	
127	Hardcoded widths are fragile. What if the terminal is wider or narrower? Tabular offers flexible width strategies:
128	
129	| Width | Meaning |
130	| ----- | ------- |
131	| `8` | Exactly 8 columns (fixed) |
132	| `{"min": 10}` | At least 10 columns; see the note below for how this is set today |
133	| `{"min": 10, "max": 30}` | Between 10 and 30, alongside a `"fill"` column |
134	| `"fill"` | Takes all remaining space |
135	| `"2fr"` | 2 parts of remaining (proportional) |
136	
137	A `{"min": ..., "max": ...}` column is resolved once, when `tabular()` or
138	`table()` builds the formatter, before any row is seen — it does not measure
139	row content. With no `"fill"` (or fractional) column in the table, any
140	leftover terminal width is added to the rightmost such column instead,
141	regardless of its `max`. Content-based growth does happen for *sub-columns*
142	(see Step 7): there, a bounded sub-column measures its own row's content and
143	resizes independently on every call to `.row(...)`. Resolving a top-level
144	column's width from every row's content — the whole table, not just one row
145	— is issue #359 in the ROB06 adopter-seams epic, which changes `tabular()` to
146	reach the whole-table width resolver that already exists internally.
147	
148	Let's make the title column expand to fill available space:
149	
150	```jinja
151	{% set t = tabular([
152	    {"name": "index", "width": 4},
153	    {"name": "status", "width": 10},
154	    {"name": "title", "width": "fill"}
155	], separator="  ") %}
156	```
157	
158	Now on an 80-column terminal:
159	
160	```text
161	1.    pending     Implement user authentication
162	2.    pending     Fix payment gateway timeout
163	3.    done        Update documentation for API v2
164	4.    pending     Review pull request #142
165	```
166	
167	On a 120-column terminal, the title column automatically expands to use the extra space.
168	
169	The layout adapts to the available space.
170	
171	---
172	
173	## Step 5: Right-Align Numbers
174	
175	Numbers and indices look better right-aligned. Use the `align` option:
176	
177	```jinja
178	{% set t = tabular([
179	    {"name": "index", "width": 4, "align": "right"},
180	    {"name": "status", "width": 10},
181	    {"name": "title", "width": "fill"}
182	], separator="  ") %}
183	```
184	
185	Output:
186	
187	```text
188	  1.  pending     Implement user authentication
189	  2.  pending     Fix payment gateway timeout
190	  3.  done        Update documentation for API v2
191	  4.  pending     Review pull request #142
192	```
193	
194	The indices now align on the right edge of their column.
195	
196	---
197	
198	## Step 6: Anchoring Columns
199	
200	Sometimes you want a column pinned to the terminal's right edge, regardless of how other columns resize. Use `anchor`:
201	
202	```jinja
203	{% set t = tabular([
204	    {"name": "index", "width": 4},
205	    {"name": "title", "width": "fill"},
206	    {"name": "status", "width": 10, "anchor": "right"}
207	], separator="  ") %}
208	```
209	
210	Now the status column is always at the right edge. If the terminal is 100 columns or 200, the status stays anchored. The fill column absorbs the extra space between fixed columns and anchored columns.
211	
212	---
213	
214	## Step 7: Sub-Columns (Distributing Space Within a Column)
215	
216	Sometimes a column contains multiple logical parts with different sizing needs. A common example: a task list where the middle column has a variable-length title and an optional tag, separated by flexible spacing.
217	
218	Without sub-columns, you can't compose `title + padding + tag` because the caller doesn't know the resolved column width. Sub-columns solve this by letting you define inner structure that is resolved per-row within the parent column's width.
219	
220	### The Problem
221	
222	Consider this layout with three columns: index (fixed), content (fill), and duration (fixed right-aligned). The content column should contain a title that grows and an optional tag that's right-aligned:
223	
224	```text
225	1.  Gallery Navigation              [feature]  4d
226	2.  Bug : Static Analysis                      8h
227	3.  Fixing Layout of Image Nav      [bug]      2d
228	```
229	
230	The tag `[feature]` must be right-aligned within the content column, with the title filling the remaining space. This is impossible with flat columns because the content column's resolved width isn't known to the template.
231	
232	### The Solution
233	
234	Define `sub_columns` on the parent column. Exactly one sub-column must be `"fill"` (the grower); the rest are Fixed or Bounded:
235	
236	```jinja
237	{% set t = tabular([
238	    {"width": 4},
239	    {"width": "fill", "sub_columns": {
240	        "columns": [
241	            {"width": "fill"},
242	            {"width": {"min": 0, "max": 30}, "align": "right"}
243	        ],
244	        "separator": " "
245	    }},
246	    {"width": 4, "align": "right"}
247	], separator="  ", width=60) %}
248	```
249	
250	Now pass nested arrays for the sub-column cells:
251	
252	```jinja
253	{% for task in tasks %}
254	{{ t.row([loop.index ~ ".", [task.title, task.tag], task.duration]) }}
255	{% endfor %}
256	```
257	
258	Each row resolves sub-column widths independently. If the tag is empty (Bounded with min=0), it takes zero width and the title fills the entire column. If the tag is present, it gets its content width (up to max=30) and the title gets the rest.
259	
260	### Sub-Column Options
261	
262	Sub-columns support the same formatting options as regular columns:
263	
264	| Option | Meaning |
265	| ------ | ------- |
266	| `width` | `"fill"`, number (fixed), or `{"min": n, "max": m}` (bounded) |
267	| `align` | `"left"` (default), `"right"`, or `"center"` |
268	| `overflow` | `"truncate"`, `"clip"`, `"wrap"`, or object form |
269	| `style` | Style name to wrap sub-cell content |
270	
271	### Rust API
272	
273	From Rust, use `CellValue::Sub` for sub-column cells:
274	
275	```rust
276	use standout_render::tabular::{
277	    TabularSpec, Col, SubCol, SubColumns, TabularFormatter, CellValue,
278	};
279	
280	let spec = TabularSpec::builder()
281	    .column(Col::fixed(4))
282	    .column(Col::fill().sub_columns(
283	        SubColumns::new(
284	            vec![SubCol::fill(), SubCol::bounded(0, 30).right()],
285	            " ",
286	        ).unwrap(),
287	    ))
288	    .column(Col::fixed(4).align(standout_render::tabular::Align::Right))
289	    .separator("  ")
290	    .build();
291	
292	let formatter = TabularFormatter::new(&spec, 60);
293	
294	let row = formatter.format_row_cells(&[
295	    CellValue::Single("1."),
296	    CellValue::Sub(vec!["Gallery Navigation", "[feature]"]),
297	    CellValue::Single("4d"),
298	]);
299	```
300	
301	`TabularFormatter::new` uses narrow ambiguous-character widths for backward
302	compatibility. To match terminals where East Asian Ambiguous glyphs occupy two
303	columns, construct the formatter explicitly:
304	
305	```rust
306	use standout_render::AmbiguousWidth;
307	
308	let formatter = TabularFormatter::with_ambiguous_width(
309	    &spec,
310	    60,
311	    AmbiguousWidth::Wide,
312	);
313	```
314	
315	The same policy is used for separators, data-driven width resolution,
316	sub-columns, borders, padding, truncation, and wrapping. MiniJinja `col`,
317	`display_width`, padding, truncation, `tabular`, and `table` operations receive
318	the renderer or application policy automatically.
319	
320	MiniJinja `tabular()` and `table()` also use the terminal width supplied by the
321	current application render context when `width` is omitted. An explicit
322	`width=...` argument takes precedence. The default terminal-width detector
323	consults a valid positive `$COLUMNS` value before probing the terminal. When
324	neither source resolves a width, both helpers use a deterministic 80-column
325	fallback.
326	
327	Policy-aware counterparts are also available for direct construction, including
328	`TabularFormatter::with_widths_and_ambiguous_width`,
329	`TabularFormatter::from_type_with_ambiguous_width`,
330	`Table::from_spec_with_ambiguous_width`, and
331	`Table::from_type_with_ambiguous_width`. Lower-level MiniJinja environments can
332	use `register_tabular_filters_with_policy`.
333	
334	In Wide mode, a decorated Unicode table treats its requested width as a hard
335	maximum. The selected Light, Heavy, Double, or Rounded border is preserved. If
336	an odd width cannot be filled by a two-column horizontal border glyph, that
337	border row may underfill by one column; it never exceeds the maximum or silently
338	switches to ASCII. Narrow table geometry is unchanged.
339	
340	### Design Constraints
341	
342	- **One level only**: Sub-columns cannot be nested recursively.
343	- **Exactly one Fill**: One sub-column must be `"fill"` (the grower). The rest must be Fixed or Bounded.
344	- **Per-row resolution**: Sub-column widths are computed independently for each row, based on actual content.
345	- **Width invariant**: The formatted sub-cell output is always exactly the parent column's width.
346	
347	---
348	
349	## Step 8: Handling Long Content
350	
351	What happens when a title is longer than its column? By default, Tabular truncates at the end with `...`. But you have options:
352	
353	### Truncate at Different Positions
354	
355	```jinja
356	{"name": "title", "width": 30, "overflow": "truncate"}                        {# "Very long title th..." #}
357	{"name": "title", "width": 30, "overflow": {"truncate": {"at": "start"}}}     {# "...itle that is long" #}
358	{"name": "title", "width": 30, "overflow": {"truncate": {"at": "middle"}}}    {# "Very long...is long" #}
359	```
360	
361	Middle truncation is perfect for file paths where both the start and end matter: `/home/user/.../important.txt`
362	
363	Semantic style tags are zero-width layout metadata. Tabular measures only the
364	visible characters, and truncation preserves balanced tags around retained
365	text. For example, truncating `prefix [match]needle[/match] suffix` at 12
366	columns produces `prefix [match]need[/match]…`; the highlighted portion remains
367	styled when rendered. Plain-text output is the only stage that strips tags.
368	
369	### Wrap to Multiple Lines
370	
371	For descriptions or messages, wrapping is often better than truncating:
372	
373	```jinja
374	{% set t = tabular([
375	    {"name": "index", "width": 4},
376	    {"name": "title", "width": 40, "overflow": "wrap"},
377	    {"name": "status", "width": 10}
378	], separator="  ") %}
379	```
380	
381	If a title exceeds 40 columns, it wraps:
382	
383	```text
384	1.    Implement comprehensive error handling    pending
385	      for all API endpoints with proper
386	      logging and user feedback
387	2.    Quick fix                                 done
388	```
389	
390	The wrapped lines are indented to align with the column.
391	
392	---
393	
394	## Step 9: Dynamic Styling Based on Values
395	
396	Here's where Tabular shines for task lists. We want status colors: green for done, yellow for pending.
397	
398	First, define styles in your theme:
399	
400	```css
401	/* styles/default.css */
402	.done { color: green; }
403	.pending { color: yellow; }
404	```
405	
406	Then use the `style_as` filter to apply styles based on the value itself:
407	
408	```jinja
409	{% set t = tabular([
410	    {"name": "index", "width": 4},
411	    {"name": "status", "width": 10},
412	    {"name": "title", "width": "fill"}
413	], separator="  ") %}
414	
415	{% for task in tasks %}
416	{{ t.row([loop.index, task.status | style_as(task.status), task.title]) }}
417	{% endfor %}
418	```
419	
420	The `style_as` filter wraps the value in style tags: `[done]done[/done]`. The rendering system then applies the green color.
421	
422	Output (with colors):
423	
424	```text
425	1.    [yellow]pending[/yellow]   Implement user authentication
426	2.    [yellow]pending[/yellow]   Fix payment gateway timeout
427	3.    [green]done[/green]        Update documentation for API v2
428	4.    [yellow]pending[/yellow]   Review pull request #142
429	```
430	
431	In the terminal, statuses appear in their respective colors, making it instantly clear which tasks need attention.
432	
433	---
434	
435	## Step 10: Column-Level Styles
436	
437	Instead of styling individual values, you can style entire columns. This is useful for de-emphasizing certain information:
438	
439	```jinja
440	{% set t = tabular([
441	    {"name": "index", "width": 4, "style": "muted"},
442	    {"name": "status", "width": 10},
443	    {"name": "title", "width": "fill"}
444	], separator="  ") %}
445	```
446	
447	Now indices appear in a muted style (typically gray), while titles and statuses remain prominent. This creates visual hierarchy.
448	
449	---
450	
451	## Step 11: Automatic Field Extraction
452	
453	Tired of manually listing `[task.title, task.status, ...]`? If your column names match your struct fields, use `row_from()`:
454	
455	```jinja
456	{% set t = tabular([
457	    {"name": "title", "width": "fill"},
458	    {"name": "status", "width": 10}
459	]) %}
460	
461	{% for task in tasks %}
462	{{ t.row_from(task) }}
463	{% endfor %}
464	```
465	
466	Tabular extracts `task.title`, `task.status`, etc. automatically. For nested fields, use `key`:
467	
468	```jinja
469	{"name": "Author", "key": "author.name", "width": 20}
470	{"name": "Email", "key": "author.email", "width": 30}
471	```
472	
473	---
474	
475	## Step 12: Adding Headers and Borders
476	
477	For a proper table with headers, switch from `tabular()` to `table()`:
478	
479	```jinja
480	{% set t = table([
481	    {"name": "#", "width": 4},
482	    {"name": "Status", "width": 10},
483	    {"name": "Title", "width": "fill"}
484	], border="rounded", header_style="bold") %}
485	
486	{{ t.header_row() }}
487	{{ t.separator_row() }}
488	{% for task in tasks %}
489	{{ t.row([loop.index, task.status, task.title]) }}
490	{% endfor %}
491	{{ t.bottom_border() }}
492	```
493	
494	Output:
495	
496	```text
497	╭──────┬────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────╮
498	│ #    │ Status     │ Title                                  │
499	├──────┼────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────┤
500	│ 1    │ pending    │ Implement user authentication          │
501	│ 2    │ pending    │ Fix payment gateway timeout            │
502	│ 3    │ done       │ Update documentation for API v2        │
503	│ 4    │ pending    │ Review pull request #142               │
504	╰──────┴────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────╯
505	```
506	
507	### Border Styles
508	
509	Choose from six border styles:
510	
511	| Style | Look |
512	| ----- | ---- |
513	| `"none"` | No borders |
514	| `"ascii"` | `+--+--+` (ASCII compatible) |
515	| `"light"` | `┌──┬──┐` |
516	| `"heavy"` | `┏━━┳━━┓` |
517	| `"double"` | `╔══╦══╗` |
518	| `"rounded"` | `╭──┬──╮` |
519	
520	### Row Separators
521	
522	For dense data, add lines between rows:
523	
524	```jinja
525	{% set t = table(columns, border="light", row_separator=true) %}
526	```
527	
528	```text
529	┌──────┬────────────────────────────────────╮
530	│ #    │ Title                              │
531	├──────┼────────────────────────────────────┤
532	│ 1    │ Implement user authentication      │
533	├──────┼────────────────────────────────────┤
534	│ 2    │ Fix payment gateway timeout        │
535	└──────┴────────────────────────────────────┘
536	```
537	
538	### Alternating Row Styles
539	
540	For long tables, alternating background colors on even/odd rows improves readability (sometimes called "zebra striping"). Pass `row_styles` to the `table()` function:
541	
542	```jinja
543	{# Default gray tint — subtle dark/light gray alternation #}
544	{% set t = table(columns, header_style="bold", row_styles=true) %}
545	
546	{# Named tint — blue, red, green, or purple #}
547	{% set t = table(columns, header_style="bold", row_styles="blue") %}
548	
549	{# Fully custom style names #}
550	{% set t = table(columns, row_styles=["my_even", "my_odd"]) %}
551	```
552	
553	The default theme includes five adaptive tints that automatically adjust to the user's light/dark terminal setting:
554	
555	| Tint | Usage | Dark mode | Light mode |
556	| -------- | ------- | ----------- | ------------ |
557	| gray | `row_styles=true` | dark gray bg | light gray bg |
558	| blue | `row_styles="blue"` | dark navy bg | lavender bg |
559	| red | `row_styles="red"` | dark crimson bg | blush bg |
560	| green | `row_styles="green"` | dark forest bg | mint bg |
561	| purple | `row_styles="purple"` | dark plum bg | lilac bg |
562	
563	The Rust API equivalent is `Table::row_styles("table_row_even", "table_row_odd")`.
564	
565	---
566	
567	## Step 13: The Complete Example
568	
569	Putting it all together, here's a polished task list:
570	
571	```jinja
572	{% set t = table([
573	    {"name": "#", "width": 4, "style": "muted"},
574	    {"name": "Status", "width": 10},
575	    {"name": "Title", "width": "fill", "overflow": {"truncate": {"at": "middle"}}}
576	], border="rounded", header_style="bold", separator=" | ") %}
577	
578	{{ t.header_row() }}
579	{{ t.separator_row() }}
580	{% for task in tasks %}
581	{{ t.row([loop.index, task.status | style_as(task.status), task.title]) }}
582	{% endfor %}
583	{{ t.bottom_border() }}
584	```
585	
586	Output (80 columns, with styling):
587	
588	```text
589	╭──────┬────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
590	│ #    │ Status     │ Title                                                 │
591	├──────┼────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
592	│ 1    │ pending    │ Implement user authentication                         │
593	│ 2    │ pending    │ Fix payment gateway timeout                           │
594	│ 3    │ done       │ Update documentation for API v2                       │
595	│ 4    │ pending    │ Review pull request #142                              │
596	╰──────┴────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
597	```
598	
599	Features in use:
600	
601	- **Rounded borders** for a modern look
602	- **Muted styling** on index column for visual hierarchy
603	- **Fill width** on title to use available space
604	- **Middle truncation** for titles that exceed the column
605	- **Dynamic status colors** via `style_as`
606	
607	---
608	
609	## Using Tabular from Rust
610	
611	Everything shown in templates is also available in Rust:
612	
613	```rust
614	use standout_render::tabular::{Col, TabularFormatter, TabularSpec};
615	
616	let spec = TabularSpec::builder()
617	    .column(Col::fixed(4).header("#").style("muted"))
618	    .column(Col::fixed(10).header("Status"))
619	    .column(Col::fill().header("Title").truncate_middle())
620	    .separator(" | ")
621	    .build();
622	
623	let formatter = TabularFormatter::new(&spec, 80);
624	
625	// Format individual rows
626	for (i, task) in tasks.iter().enumerate() {
627	    let row = formatter.format_row(&[
628	        &(i + 1).to_string(),
629	        &task.status.to_string(),
630	        &task.title,
631	    ]);
632	    println!("{}", row);
633	}
634	```
635	
636	---
637	
638	## Summary
639	
640	Tabular transforms raw data into polished, scannable output with minimal effort:
641	
642	1. **Start simple** - use `col` filter for quick alignment
643	2. **Structure with `tabular()`** - centralize column definitions
644	3. **Flex with widths** - use `fill`, bounded ranges, and fractions
645	4. **Align content** - right-align numbers and dates
646	5. **Anchor columns** - pin important data to edges
647	6. **Handle overflow** - truncate intelligently or wrap
648	7. **Add visual hierarchy** - style columns and values dynamically
649	8. **Extract automatically** - let `row_from()` pull fields from structs
650	9. **Decorate as tables** - add borders, headers, and separators
651	
652	The declarative approach means your layout adapts to terminal width, applies the explicitly selected Unicode ambiguous-width policy consistently, and remains maintainable as your data evolves.
653	
654	For complete API details, see the [API documentation](https://docs.rs/standout-render).
655

# Introduction to Tabular

Polished terminal output requires two things: good formatting (see [Rendering Introduction](intro-to-rendering.md)) and good layouts. For text-only, non-interactive output, layout mostly means aligning things vertically and controlling how multiple pieces of information are presented together.

Tabular provides a declarative column system with powerful primitives for sizing (fixed, range, fill, fractions), positioning (anchor to right), overflow handling (clip, wrap, truncate), cell alignment, and automated per-column styling.

Tabular is not only about tables. Any listing where items have multiple fields that benefit from vertical alignment is a good candidate—log entries with authors, timestamps, and messages; file listings with names, sizes, and dates; task lists with IDs, titles, and statuses. Add headers, separators, and borders to a tabular layout, and you have a table.

**Key capabilities:**

- **Flexible sizing**: Fixed widths, min/max ranges, fill remaining space, fractional proportions
- **Smart truncation**: Truncate at start, middle, or end with custom ellipsis
- **Word wrapping**: Wrap long content across multiple lines with proper alignment
- **Unicode-aware**: CJK characters, combining marks, and ANSI codes handled correctly
- **Dynamic styling**: Style columns or individual values based on content

In this guide, we will walk from a simple listing to a polished table, exploring the available features.

**See Also:**

- [Introduction to Rendering](intro-to-rendering.md) - templates and styles overview
- [Styling System](../topics/styling-system.md) - themes and adaptive styles

---

## Our Example: Task List

We'll build the output for a task list. This is a perfect Tabular use case: each task has an index, title, and status. We want them aligned, readable, and visually clear at a glance.

Here's our data:

```rust
use serde::Serialize;

#[derive(Clone, Serialize)]
#[serde(rename_all = "lowercase")]
pub enum Status { Pending, Done }

#[derive(Clone, Serialize)]
struct Task {
    title: String,
    status: Status,
}

let tasks = vec![
    Task { title: "Implement user authentication".into(), status: Status::Pending },
    Task { title: "Fix payment gateway timeout".into(), status: Status::Pending },
    Task { title: "Update documentation for API v2".into(), status: Status::Done },
    Task { title: "Review pull request #142".into(), status: Status::Pending },
];
```

Let's progressively build this from raw output to a polished, professional listing.

---

## Step 1: The Problem with Plain Output

Without any formatting, a naive approach might look like this:

```jinja
{% for task in tasks %}
{{ loop.index }}. {{ task.title }} {{ task.status }}
{% endfor %}
```

Output:

```text
1. Implement user authentication pending
2. Fix payment gateway timeout pending
3. Update documentation for API v2 done
4. Review pull request #142 pending
```

This is barely readable. Fields run together, nothing aligns, and scanning the list requires mental parsing of each line. Let's fix that.

---

## Step 2: Basic Column Alignment with `col`

The simplest improvement is the `col` filter. It pads (or truncates) each value to a fixed width:

```jinja
{% for task in tasks %}
{{ loop.index | col(4) }}  {{ task.status | col(10) }}  {{ task.title | col(40) }}
{% endfor %}
```

Output:

```text
1.    pending     Implement user authentication
2.    pending     Fix payment gateway timeout
3.    done        Update documentation for API v2
4.    pending     Review pull request #142
```

Already much better. Each column aligns vertically, making it easy to scan. But we've hardcoded widths, and if a title is too long, it gets truncated with `...`.

> **Key insight:** The `col` filter handles Unicode correctly. CJK characters count as 2 columns, combining marks don't add width, and ANSI escape codes are preserved but not counted.

---

## Step 3: Structured Layout with `tabular()`

For more control, use the `tabular()` function. This creates a formatter that you configure once and use for all rows:

```jinja
{% set t = tabular([
    {"name": "index", "width": 4},
    {"name": "status", "width": 10},
    {"name": "title", "width": 40}
], separator="  ") %}

{% for task in tasks %}
{{ t.row([loop.index, task.status, task.title]) }}
{% endfor %}
```

The output looks the same, but now the column definitions are centralized. This becomes powerful when we start adding features.

---

## Step 4: Flexible Widths

Hardcoded widths are fragile. What if the terminal is wider or narrower? Tabular offers flexible width strategies:

| Width | Meaning |
| ----- | ------- |
| `8` | Exactly 8 columns (fixed) |
| `{"min": 10}` | At least 10 columns; see the note below for how this is set today |
| `{"min": 10, "max": 30}` | Between 10 and 30, alongside a `"fill"` column |
| `"fill"` | Takes all remaining space |
| `"2fr"` | 2 parts of remaining (proportional) |

A `{"min": ..., "max": ...}` column is resolved once, when `tabular()` or
`table()` builds the formatter, before any row is seen — it does not measure
row content. With no `"fill"` (or fractional) column in the table, any
leftover terminal width is added to the rightmost such column instead,
regardless of its `max`. Content-based growth does happen for *sub-columns*
(see Step 7): there, a bounded sub-column measures its own row's content and
resizes independently on every call to `.row(...)`. Resolving a top-level
column's width from every row's content — the whole table, not just one row
— is issue #359 in the ROB06 adopter-seams epic, which changes `tabular()` to
reach the whole-table width resolver that already exists internally.

Let's make the title column expand to fill available space:

```jinja
{% set t = tabular([
    {"name": "index", "width": 4},
    {"name": "status", "width": 10},
    {"name": "title", "width": "fill"}
], separator="  ") %}
```

Now on an 80-column terminal:

```text
1.    pending     Implement user authentication
2.    pending     Fix payment gateway timeout
3.    done        Update documentation for API v2
4.    pending     Review pull request #142
```

On a 120-column terminal, the title column automatically expands to use the extra space.

The layout adapts to the available space.

---

## Step 5: Right-Align Numbers

Numbers and indices look better right-aligned. Use the `align` option:

```jinja
{% set t = tabular([
    {"name": "index", "width": 4, "align": "right"},
    {"name": "status", "width": 10},
    {"name": "title", "width": "fill"}
], separator="  ") %}
```

Output:

```text
  1.  pending     Implement user authentication
  2.  pending     Fix payment gateway timeout
  3.  done        Update documentation for API v2
  4.  pending     Review pull request #142
```

The indices now align on the right edge of their column.

---

## Step 6: Anchoring Columns

Sometimes you want a column pinned to the terminal's right edge, regardless of how other columns resize. Use `anchor`:

```jinja
{% set t = tabular([
    {"name": "index", "width": 4},
    {"name": "title", "width": "fill"},
    {"name": "status", "width": 10, "anchor": "right"}
], separator="  ") %}
```

Now the status column is always at the right edge. If the terminal is 100 columns or 200, the status stays anchored. The fill column absorbs the extra space between fixed columns and anchored columns.

---

## Step 7: Sub-Columns (Distributing Space Within a Column)

Sometimes a column contains multiple logical parts with different sizing needs. A common example: a task list where the middle column has a variable-length title and an optional tag, separated by flexible spacing.

Without sub-columns, you can't compose `title + padding + tag` because the caller doesn't know the resolved column width. Sub-columns solve this by letting you define inner structure that is resolved per-row within the parent column's width.

### The Problem

Consider this layout with three columns: index (fixed), content (fill), and duration (fixed right-aligned). The content column should contain a title that grows and an optional tag that's right-aligned:

```text
1.  Gallery Navigation              [feature]  4d
2.  Bug : Static Analysis                      8h
3.  Fixing Layout of Image Nav      [bug]      2d
```

The tag `[feature]` must be right-aligned within the content column, with the title filling the remaining space. This is impossible with flat columns because the content column's resolved width isn't known to the template.

### The Solution

Define `sub_columns` on the parent column. Exactly one sub-column must be `"fill"` (the grower); the rest are Fixed or Bounded:

```jinja
{% set t = tabular([
    {"width": 4},
    {"width": "fill", "sub_columns": {
        "columns": [
            {"width": "fill"},
            {"width": {"min": 0, "max": 30}, "align": "right"}
        ],
        "separator": " "
    }},
    {"width": 4, "align": "right"}
], separator="  ", width=60) %}
```

Now pass nested arrays for the sub-column cells:

```jinja
{% for task in tasks %}
{{ t.row([loop.index ~ ".", [task.title, task.tag], task.duration]) }}
{% endfor %}
```

Each row resolves sub-column widths independently. If the tag is empty (Bounded with min=0), it takes zero width and the title fills the entire column. If the tag is present, it gets its content width (up to max=30) and the title gets the rest.

### Sub-Column Options

Sub-columns support the same formatting options as regular columns:

| Option | Meaning |
| ------ | ------- |
| `width` | `"fill"`, number (fixed), or `{"min": n, "max": m}` (bounded) |
| `align` | `"left"` (default), `"right"`, or `"center"` |
| `overflow` | `"truncate"`, `"clip"`, `"wrap"`, or object form |
| `style` | Style name to wrap sub-cell content |

### Rust API

From Rust, use `CellValue::Sub` for sub-column cells:

```rust
use standout_render::tabular::{
    TabularSpec, Col, SubCol, SubColumns, TabularFormatter, CellValue,
};

let spec = TabularSpec::builder()
    .column(Col::fixed(4))
    .column(Col::fill().sub_columns(
        SubColumns::new(
            vec![SubCol::fill(), SubCol::bounded(0, 30).right()],
            " ",
        ).unwrap(),
    ))
    .column(Col::fixed(4).align(standout_render::tabular::Align::Right))
    .separator("  ")
    .build();

let formatter = TabularFormatter::new(&spec, 60);

let row = formatter.format_row_cells(&[
    CellValue::Single("1."),
    CellValue::Sub(vec!["Gallery Navigation", "[feature]"]),
    CellValue::Single("4d"),
]);
```

`TabularFormatter::new` uses narrow ambiguous-character widths for backward
compatibility. To match terminals where East Asian Ambiguous glyphs occupy two
columns, construct the formatter explicitly:

```rust
use standout_render::AmbiguousWidth;

let formatter = TabularFormatter::with_ambiguous_width(
    &spec,
    60,
    AmbiguousWidth::Wide,
);
```

The same policy is used for separators, data-driven width resolution,
sub-columns, borders, padding, truncation, and wrapping. MiniJinja `col`,
`display_width`, padding, truncation, `tabular`, and `table` operations receive
the renderer or application policy automatically.

MiniJinja `tabular()` and `table()` also use the terminal width supplied by the
current application render context when `width` is omitted. An explicit
`width=...` argument takes precedence. The default terminal-width detector
consults a valid positive `$COLUMNS` value before probing the terminal. When
neither source resolves a width, both helpers use a deterministic 80-column
fallback.

Policy-aware counterparts are also available for direct construction, including
`TabularFormatter::with_widths_and_ambiguous_width`,
`TabularFormatter::from_type_with_ambiguous_width`,
`Table::from_spec_with_ambiguous_width`, and
`Table::from_type_with_ambiguous_width`. Lower-level MiniJinja environments can
use `register_tabular_filters_with_policy`.

In Wide mode, a decorated Unicode table treats its requested width as a hard
maximum. The selected Light, Heavy, Double, or Rounded border is preserved. If
an odd width cannot be filled by a two-column horizontal border glyph, that
border row may underfill by one column; it never exceeds the maximum or silently
switches to ASCII. Narrow table geometry is unchanged.

### Design Constraints

- **One level only**: Sub-columns cannot be nested recursively.
- **Exactly one Fill**: One sub-column must be `"fill"` (the grower). The rest must be Fixed or Bounded.
- **Per-row resolution**: Sub-column widths are computed independently for each row, based on actual content.
- **Width invariant**: The formatted sub-cell output is always exactly the parent column's width.

---

## Step 8: Handling Long Content

What happens when a title is longer than its column? By default, Tabular truncates at the end with `...`. But you have options:

### Truncate at Different Positions

```jinja
{"name": "title", "width": 30, "overflow": "truncate"}                        {# "Very long title th..." #}
{"name": "title", "width": 30, "overflow": {"truncate": {"at": "start"}}}     {# "...itle that is long" #}
{"name": "title", "width": 30, "overflow": {"truncate": {"at": "middle"}}}    {# "Very long...is long" #}
```

Middle truncation is perfect for file paths where both the start and end matter: `/home/user/.../important.txt`

Semantic style tags are zero-width layout metadata. Tabular measures only the
visible characters, and truncation preserves balanced tags around retained
text. For example, truncating `prefix [match]needle[/match] suffix` at 12
columns produces `prefix [match]need[/match]…`; the highlighted portion remains
styled when rendered. Plain-text output is the only stage that strips tags.

### Wrap to Multiple Lines

For descriptions or messages, wrapping is often better than truncating:

```jinja
{% set t = tabular([
    {"name": "index", "width": 4},
    {"name": "title", "width": 40, "overflow": "wrap"},
    {"name": "status", "width": 10}
], separator="  ") %}
```

If a title exceeds 40 columns, it wraps:

```text
1.    Implement comprehensive error handling    pending
      for all API endpoints with proper
      logging and user feedback
2.    Quick fix                                 done
```

The wrapped lines are indented to align with the column.

---

## Step 9: Dynamic Styling Based on Values

Here's where Tabular shines for task lists. We want status colors: green for done, yellow for pending.

First, define styles in your theme:

```css
/* styles/default.css */
.done { color: green; }
.pending { color: yellow; }
```

Then use the `style_as` filter to apply styles based on the value itself:

```jinja
{% set t = tabular([
    {"name": "index", "width": 4},
    {"name": "status", "width": 10},
    {"name": "title", "width": "fill"}
], separator="  ") %}

{% for task in tasks %}
{{ t.row([loop.index, task.status | style_as(task.status), task.title]) }}
{% endfor %}
```

The `style_as` filter wraps the value in style tags: `[done]done[/done]`. The rendering system then applies the green color.

Output (with colors):

```text
1.    [yellow]pending[/yellow]   Implement user authentication
2.    [yellow]pending[/yellow]   Fix payment gateway timeout
3.    [green]done[/green]        Update documentation for API v2
4.    [yellow]pending[/yellow]   Review pull request #142
```

In the terminal, statuses appear in their respective colors, making it instantly clear which tasks need attention.

---

## Step 10: Column-Level Styles

Instead of styling individual values, you can style entire columns. This is useful for de-emphasizing certain information:

```jinja
{% set t = tabular([
    {"name": "index", "width": 4, "style": "muted"},
    {"name": "status", "width": 10},
    {"name": "title", "width": "fill"}
], separator="  ") %}
```

Now indices appear in a muted style (typically gray), while titles and statuses remain prominent. This creates visual hierarchy.

---

## Step 11: Automatic Field Extraction

Tired of manually listing `[task.title, task.status, ...]`? If your column names match your struct fields, use `row_from()`:

```jinja
{% set t = tabular([
    {"name": "title", "width": "fill"},
    {"name": "status", "width": 10}
]) %}

{% for task in tasks %}
{{ t.row_from(task) }}
{% endfor %}
```

Tabular extracts `task.title`, `task.status`, etc. automatically. For nested fields, use `key`:

```jinja
{"name": "Author", "key": "author.name", "width": 20}
{"name": "Email", "key": "author.email", "width": 30}
```

---

## Step 12: Adding Headers and Borders

For a proper table with headers, switch from `tabular()` to `table()`:

```jinja
{% set t = table([
    {"name": "#", "width": 4},
    {"name": "Status", "width": 10},
    {"name": "Title", "width": "fill"}
], border="rounded", header_style="bold") %}

{{ t.header_row() }}
{{ t.separator_row() }}
{% for task in tasks %}
{{ t.row([loop.index, task.status, task.title]) }}
{% endfor %}
{{ t.bottom_border() }}
```

Output:

```text
╭──────┬────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ #    │ Status     │ Title                                  │
├──────┼────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 1    │ pending    │ Implement user authentication          │
│ 2    │ pending    │ Fix payment gateway timeout            │
│ 3    │ done       │ Update documentation for API v2        │
│ 4    │ pending    │ Review pull request #142               │
╰──────┴────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────╯
```

### Border Styles

Choose from six border styles:

| Style | Look |
| ----- | ---- |
| `"none"` | No borders |
| `"ascii"` | `+--+--+` (ASCII compatible) |
| `"light"` | `┌──┬──┐` |
| `"heavy"` | `┏━━┳━━┓` |
| `"double"` | `╔══╦══╗` |
| `"rounded"` | `╭──┬──╮` |

### Row Separators

For dense data, add lines between rows:

```jinja
{% set t = table(columns, border="light", row_separator=true) %}
```

```text
┌──────┬────────────────────────────────────╮
│ #    │ Title                              │
├──────┼────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 1    │ Implement user authentication      │
├──────┼────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 2    │ Fix payment gateway timeout        │
└──────┴────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Alternating Row Styles

For long tables, alternating background colors on even/odd rows improves readability (sometimes called "zebra striping"). Pass `row_styles` to the `table()` function:

```jinja
{# Default gray tint — subtle dark/light gray alternation #}
{% set t = table(columns, header_style="bold", row_styles=true) %}

{# Named tint — blue, red, green, or purple #}
{% set t = table(columns, header_style="bold", row_styles="blue") %}

{# Fully custom style names #}
{% set t = table(columns, row_styles=["my_even", "my_odd"]) %}
```

The default theme includes five adaptive tints that automatically adjust to the user's light/dark terminal setting:

| Tint | Usage | Dark mode | Light mode |
| -------- | ------- | ----------- | ------------ |
| gray | `row_styles=true` | dark gray bg | light gray bg |
| blue | `row_styles="blue"` | dark navy bg | lavender bg |
| red | `row_styles="red"` | dark crimson bg | blush bg |
| green | `row_styles="green"` | dark forest bg | mint bg |
| purple | `row_styles="purple"` | dark plum bg | lilac bg |

The Rust API equivalent is `Table::row_styles("table_row_even", "table_row_odd")`.

---

## Step 13: The Complete Example

Putting it all together, here's a polished task list:

```jinja
{% set t = table([
    {"name": "#", "width": 4, "style": "muted"},
    {"name": "Status", "width": 10},
    {"name": "Title", "width": "fill", "overflow": {"truncate": {"at": "middle"}}}
], border="rounded", header_style="bold", separator=" | ") %}

{{ t.header_row() }}
{{ t.separator_row() }}
{% for task in tasks %}
{{ t.row([loop.index, task.status | style_as(task.status), task.title]) }}
{% endfor %}
{{ t.bottom_border() }}
```

Output (80 columns, with styling):

```text
╭──────┬────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ #    │ Status     │ Title                                                 │
├──────┼────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 1    │ pending    │ Implement user authentication                         │
│ 2    │ pending    │ Fix payment gateway timeout                           │
│ 3    │ done       │ Update documentation for API v2                       │
│ 4    │ pending    │ Review pull request #142                              │
╰──────┴────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
```

Features in use:

- **Rounded borders** for a modern look
- **Muted styling** on index column for visual hierarchy
- **Fill width** on title to use available space
- **Middle truncation** for titles that exceed the column
- **Dynamic status colors** via `style_as`

---

## Using Tabular from Rust

Everything shown in templates is also available in Rust:

```rust
use standout_render::tabular::{Col, TabularFormatter, TabularSpec};

let spec = TabularSpec::builder()
    .column(Col::fixed(4).header("#").style("muted"))
    .column(Col::fixed(10).header("Status"))
    .column(Col::fill().header("Title").truncate_middle())
    .separator(" | ")
    .build();

let formatter = TabularFormatter::new(&spec, 80);

// Format individual rows
for (i, task) in tasks.iter().enumerate() {
    let row = formatter.format_row(&[
        &(i + 1).to_string(),
        &task.status.to_string(),
        &task.title,
    ]);
    println!("{}", row);
}
```

---

## Summary

Tabular transforms raw data into polished, scannable output with minimal effort:

1. **Start simple** - use `col` filter for quick alignment
2. **Structure with `tabular()`** - centralize column definitions
3. **Flex with widths** - use `fill`, bounded ranges, and fractions
4. **Align content** - right-align numbers and dates
5. **Anchor columns** - pin important data to edges
6. **Handle overflow** - truncate intelligently or wrap
7. **Add visual hierarchy** - style columns and values dynamically
8. **Extract automatically** - let `row_from()` pull fields from structs
9. **Decorate as tables** - add borders, headers, and separators

The declarative approach means your layout adapts to terminal width, applies the explicitly selected Unicode ambiguous-width policy consistently, and remains maintainable as your data evolves.

For complete API details, see the [API documentation](https://docs.rs/standout-render).

1	# List Views
2	
3	Most CLI commands that print a collection share the same shape: an optional
4	intro line, the items, an optional list of messages (warnings, info), and an
5	optional summary of how many items were filtered out of a larger total. The
6	`list_view` builder in `standout::views` captures that shape once so handlers
7	stop reassembling it by hand, and `#[dispatch(list_view)]` wires the result to
8	the framework's built-in list template without a project-owned template file.
9	
10	Reach for it whenever a handler returns "here are N things" — a `list`,
11	`search`, or `status` command — and the result needs more than a bare `Vec<T>`:
12	an intro line, a filter summary, or per-item messages.
13	
14	## Where it lives
15	
16	`list_view`, `ListViewBuilder`, and `ListViewResult` live in
17	`standout::views`, a module (`pub mod views`) rather than a crate-root
18	re-export:
19	
20	```rust
21	use standout::views::{list_view, ListViewBuilder, ListViewResult};
22	```
23	
24	## The builder
25	
26	```rust
27	pub fn list_view<T>(items: impl IntoIterator<Item = T>) -> ListViewBuilder<T>;
28	```
29	
30	`ListViewBuilder<T>` accepts items in any order and returns itself, so calls
31	chain:
32	
33	| Method | Effect |
34	| --- | --- |
35	| `.intro(text)` | A line shown before the items |
36	| `.ending(text)` | A line shown after the items |
37	| `.message(level, text)` | Attaches a `Message` at the given `MessageLevel` |
38	| `.info(text)` | Shortcut for `.message(MessageLevel::Info, text)` |
39	| `.success(text)` | Shortcut for `.message(MessageLevel::Success, text)` |
40	| `.warning(text)` | Shortcut for `.message(MessageLevel::Warning, text)` |
41	| `.error(text)` | Shortcut for `.message(MessageLevel::Error, text)` |
42	| `.total_count(n)` | Records the unfiltered total, for a "showing X of Y" summary |

# List Views

Most CLI commands that print a collection share the same shape: an optional
intro line, the items, an optional list of messages (warnings, info), and an
optional summary of how many items were filtered out of a larger total. The
`list_view` builder in `standout::views` captures that shape once so handlers
stop reassembling it by hand, and `#[dispatch(list_view)]` wires the result to
the framework's built-in list template without a project-owned template file.

Reach for it whenever a handler returns "here are N things" — a `list`,
`search`, or `status` command — and the result needs more than a bare `Vec<T>`:
an intro line, a filter summary, or per-item messages.

## Where it lives

`list_view`, `ListViewBuilder`, and `ListViewResult` live in
`standout::views`, a module (`pub mod views`) rather than a crate-root
re-export:

```rust
use standout::views::{list_view, ListViewBuilder, ListViewResult};
```

## The builder

```rust
pub fn list_view<T>(items: impl IntoIterator<Item = T>) -> ListViewBuilder<T>;
```

`ListViewBuilder<T>` accepts items in any order and returns itself, so calls
chain:

| Method | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `.intro(text)` | A line shown before the items |
| `.ending(text)` | A line shown after the items |
| `.message(level, text)` | Attaches a `Message` at the given `MessageLevel` |
| `.info(text)` | Shortcut for `.message(MessageLevel::Info, text)` |
| `.success(text)` | Shortcut for `.message(MessageLevel::Success, text)` |
| `.warning(text)` | Shortcut for `.message(MessageLevel::Warning, text)` |
| `.error(text)` | Shortcut for `.message(MessageLevel::Error, text)` |
| `.total_count(n)` | Records the unfiltered total, for a "showing X of Y" summary |
| `.filter_summary(text)` | A human-readable description of the active filter |
| `.tabular_spec(spec)` | Attaches a `TabularSpec` directly (usually left to `#[dispatch(list_view, item_type = "...")]` instead) |
| `.build()` | Consumes the builder and returns a `ListViewResult<T>` |

## The result

```rust
pub struct ListViewResult<T> {
    pub items: Vec<T>,
    pub intro: Option<String>,
    pub ending: Option<String>,
    pub messages: Vec<Message>,
    pub total_count: Option<usize>,
    pub filter_summary: Option<String>,
    pub tabular_spec: Option<TabularSpec>,
}
```

`ListViewResult<T>` implements `Serialize` (fields that are `None` or empty
are skipped, so `--output json` stays uncluttered), `Default` (an empty list
with every optional field unset), and carries `.is_empty()` and `.len()`
methods that read `items` directly.

Because it derives `Serialize` rather than requiring one, `ListViewResult<T>`
is itself a valid handler return type: a handler can return
`HandlerResult<ListViewResult<Task>>` and wrap it in `Output::Render` like any
other structured output. See
[Handler Contract](../crates/dispatch/topics/handler-contract.md) for the
`Output` enum and the render pipeline it feeds.

## Connecting to `#[dispatch(list_view)]`

The `Dispatch` derive has a `list_view` variant attribute that does two
things to a variant's handler:

- It sets the command's template to the framework-provided
  `standout/list-view` template, unless the variant also sets
  `#[dispatch(template_name = "...")]`, in which case that name wins.
- If `item_type = "..."` names a type implementing `Tabular`, the derive
  wraps the handler so that, on a successful `Output::Render(list_view_result)`,
  it stamps `list_view_result.tabular_spec` with `<ItemType as Tabular>::tabular_spec()`
  before rendering. The handler itself never has to know about the column
  layout.

Handlers under `#[dispatch(list_view)]` can be either the two-argument shape
(`fn(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<ListViewResult<T>>`) or,
with `#[dispatch(simple)]` added, a single-argument shape
(`fn(&ArgMatches) -> HandlerResult<ListViewResult<T>>`). Both are wrapped the
same way.

## Worked example

```rust
use clap::{ArgMatches, Subcommand};
use serde::Serialize;
use standout::cli::{CommandContext, Dispatch, HandlerResult, Output};
use standout::views::list_view;
use standout::{Tabular, TabularRow};

#[derive(Serialize, Tabular, TabularRow, Clone)]
struct Task {
    #[col(width = 5)]
    id: u32,
    #[col(width = 20)]
    name: String,
}

mod handlers {
    use super::*;

    pub fn list(
        _matches: &ArgMatches,
        _ctx: &CommandContext,
    ) -> HandlerResult<standout::views::ListViewResult<Task>> {
        let tasks = vec![Task {
            id: 1,
            name: "Write docs".to_string(),
        }];
        Ok(Output::Render(list_view(tasks).build()))
    }
}

#[derive(Subcommand, Dispatch)]
#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
enum Commands {
    #[dispatch(list_view, item_type = "Task")]
    List,
}
```

Running `list` renders the framework's list template with `Task`'s column
widths already attached; `--output json` serializes the same
`ListViewResult<Task>`, `tabular_spec` included, with no template involved.
An empty `items` vec renders the template's "No items found" branch rather
than an empty table.

## Disabling the framework template

`App::builder().include_framework_templates(false)` refuses to build if a
command names `standout/list-view` (or any other framework template) without
supplying a replacement — a project can opt out of the built-in list layout,
but only by registering its own template under the same name.

1	# The `#[dispatch(…)]` and `#[handler]` Reference
2	
3	Two macros carry the blessed idiom. `#[derive(Dispatch)]` on an enum binds
4	command names to handler functions; `#[handler]` on a function turns it into
5	something the dispatcher can call. This page is the complete list of what each
6	one accepts.
7	
8	Both name mappings on this page — a variant name to a command name, and a
9	parameter name to a clap argument id — are contract, because they decide the
10	words a user types in a shell script. See
11	[What Is Contract](stability.md#4-the-two-name-mappings-a-user-types-on-the-command-line).
12	
13	## `#[derive(Dispatch)]`
14	
15	### The container attribute
16	
17	One attribute goes on the enum, and it is required:
18	
19	```rust,ignore
20	#[derive(Dispatch)]
21	#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
22	enum Commands { /* … */ }
23	```
24	
25	`handlers = <module path>` names the module the derive looks each variant's
26	handler up in. Without it, expansion fails with `missing #[dispatch(handlers =
27	path)] attribute`.
28	
29	### From a variant name to a command name
30	
31	A variant registers under its **kebab-case** name — `ListUnits` becomes
32	`list-units` — which is the spelling clap's own derive gives the subcommand.
33	`#[dispatch(name = "…")]` renames one variant.
34	
35	A `name` may not be empty and may not contain `.`: dispatch splits registration
36	paths on `.`, so such a name would register a nested path no clap subcommand
37	declares. Nesting is `#[dispatch(nested)]`, below.
38	
39	A registered path that no clap subcommand can reach is a loud error naming the
40	path, raised by `App::run` and `App::verify_command` before dispatch.
41	
42	### From a variant name to a handler function
43	
44	The handler is looked up under the variant's **snake_case** name in the
45	`handlers` module — `ListUnits` calls `handlers::list_units`. Two attributes
46	change that:
47	
48	- `#[dispatch(pure)]` appends `__handler`, so the derive calls
49	  `handlers::list_units__handler` — the wrapper `#[handler]` generated. Use it
50	  whenever the handler function carries `#[handler]`, which is the blessed
51	  style. The derive registers through a closure taking `HandlerResult<T>`, so a
52	  `pure` handler must be annotated `-> Result<Output<T>, E>` or
53	  `-> Result<(), E>`; a plain `-> Result<T, E>` fails expansion. See
54	  [what `#[handler]` generates](#what-handler-generates).
55	- `#[dispatch(handler = <path>)]` names the function outright and ignores the
56	  inferred name.
57	
58	The two are mutually exclusive, and expansion rejects the pair with a message
59	naming both. Without `pure`, the derive calls the named function directly, so
60	that function must already have the dispatch signature.
61	
62	### Every variant attribute
63	
64	Several `#[dispatch(…)]` attributes may sit on one variant; they merge before
65	anything reads them.
66	
67	| Attribute | Form | What it does |
68	| --- | --- | --- |
69	| `name` | `name = "…"` | Registers the command under this name instead of the variant's kebab-case name. Not empty, no `.`. |
70	| `handler` | `handler = <path>` | Calls this function instead of the inferred one. Excludes `pure`. |
71	| `pure` | flag | The handler carries `#[handler]`: append `__handler` to the inferred name. Excludes `handler` and `simple`. |
72	| `simple` | flag | The handler takes only `&ArgMatches`, with no `&CommandContext`. Excludes `pure`. |
73	| `nested` | flag | The variant is a subcommand group. Requires a single-field tuple variant wrapping another `Dispatch` enum. |
74	| `skip` | flag | Registers nothing for this variant. |
75	| `default` | flag | Runs this command on a naked invocation. At most one variant per enum. |
76	| `template_name` | `template_name = "…"` | Names the template registry entry instead of using the convention. Excludes `silent`, `binary` and `structured_only`. |
77	| `silent` | flag | The command renders nothing. Excludes `binary`, `structured_only`, `template_name`. |
78	| `binary` | flag | The command writes bytes rather than a rendered page. Same exclusions. |
79	| `structured_only` | flag | The command has output only in the structured modes. Same exclusions. |
80	| `list_view` | flag | Renders through the framework's built-in `standout/list-view` template, unless `template_name` also appears, and attaches a tabular spec to the handler's `Output::Render`. |
81	| `item_type` | `item_type = "…"` | Names the `Tabular`-implementing item type `list_view` builds its spec from. |
82	| `questionnaire` | `questionnaire = <path>` | Resolves this questionnaire type before the handler runs. |
83	| `pre_dispatch` | `pre_dispatch = <path>` | Runs this hook before the handler. |
84	| `post_dispatch` | `post_dispatch = <path>` | Runs this hook after the handler, before rendering. |
85	| `post_output` | `post_output = <path>` | Runs this hook after the output is produced. |
86	| `pipe_to` | `pipe_to = "…"` | Sends the output to this command and keeps the original. |
87	| `pipe_through` | `pipe_through = "…"` | Replaces the output with this command's stdout. |
88	| `pipe_to_clipboard` | flag | Sends the output to the clipboard. |
89	
90	An unrecognized key fails expansion with a message listing every key above.
91	
92	### Nested commands
93	
94	`#[dispatch(nested)]` marks a variant that wraps another `Dispatch` enum:
95	
96	```rust,ignore
97	#[derive(Dispatch)]
98	#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
99	enum Commands {
100	    #[dispatch(nested)]
101	    Pr(PrCommands),
102	}
103	```
104	
105	The derive registers the group rather than a command, and the inner enum's own
106	variants register beneath it. Registration paths are dot-joined as the
107	recursion descends, so `pr checks list` registers the path `pr.checks.list`.
108	
109	### How a command finds its template
110	
111	With no `template_name` and no absence marker (`silent`, `binary`,
112	`structured_only`), the template name **is** the registration path with each
113	`.` replaced by `/`, and **no extension appended**:
114	
115	| Registration path | Template name |
116	| --- | --- |
117	| `list` | `list` |
118	| `pr.checks.list` | `pr/checks/list` |
119	
120	The registry then resolves that name against `.jinja`, `.jinja2`, `.j2`,
121	`.stpl` and `.txt`, in that priority order — so a nested `pr checks list`
122	command is rendered by `src/templates/pr/checks/list.jinja`. A name may be
123	looked up with or without an extension; the extension is stripped and the base
124	name retried.
125	
126	`#[dispatch(template_name = "…")]` replaces that name with a registry entry you
127	choose, which is how two commands share one template.
128	
129	## `#[handler]`
130	
131	### Parameter attributes
132	
133	Every typed parameter carries one of four attributes, references included: the
134	macro reads the value out of `ArgMatches` (or hands over the dispatcher's own
135	reference) by the attribute, never by the type, so a `&CommandContext` still
136	needs `#[ctx]` and an `&ArgMatches` still needs `#[matches]`.
137	
138	| Attribute | Type | Where the value comes from |
139	| --- | --- | --- |
140	| `#[flag]` | `bool` | `matches.get_flag(id)` |
141	| `#[arg]` | `T` | a required argument |
142	| `#[arg]` | `Option<T>` | an optional argument |
143	| `#[arg]` | `Vec<T>` | a repeated argument |
144	| `#[ctx]` | `&CommandContext` | the dispatcher |
145	| `#[matches]` | `&ArgMatches` | the dispatcher, unparsed |
146	
147	### From a parameter name to a clap argument id
148	
149	**Underscores become hyphens.** A parameter named `no_legend` reads the
150	argument whose id is `no-legend`.
151	
152	Clap's own derive ids an argument by the field name it comes from, so the two
153	disagree unless one of them says so. Either side can:
154	
155	```rust,ignore
156	#[arg(id = "no-legend")]        // on the clap-derive field
157	no_legend: bool,
158	
159	#[flag(name = "no_legend")]     // on the handler parameter
160	no_legend: bool,
161	```
162	
163	`app.verify_command(&cmd)` reports the mismatch at build time rather than
164	leaving it to a runtime `get_flag` panic.
165	
166	A parameter named with a raw identifier drops the `r#` first, the way clap's
167	derive drops it from a field name: `r#type` reads the argument id `type`.
168	
169	### What `#[handler]` generates
170	
171	For `fn list`, four items:
172	
173	| Item | What it is |
174	| --- | --- |
175	| `list` | the original function, unchanged apart from the parameter attributes being removed — still directly callable from a test |
176	| `list__handler(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext)` | the wrapper that extracts the arguments and calls `list`. It returns **the function's own annotated return type**, verbatim |
177	| `list__expected_args() -> Vec<ExpectedArg>` | what `verify_command` reads |
178	| `list_Handler` | a unit struct implementing `Handler` — the registrable item |
179	
180	The `Result<T, E>` to `Output::Render` wrap happens inside `Handler::handle`,
181	not inside `list__handler`, and that is what makes the two registration methods
182	accept different things. `AppBuilder::command_with` takes an `impl Handler`, so
183	`handlers::list_Handler` works for any of the three return shapes.
184	`GroupBuilder::command_with` — which is what `#[derive(Dispatch)]` reaches —
185	takes a closure returning `HandlerResult<T>`, so it accepts
186	`handlers::list__handler` only when the function was annotated
187	`-> Result<Output<T>, E>` or `-> Result<(), E>`. The un-suffixed
188	`handlers::list` is registrable through neither.
189	
190	See the [handler contract](../crates/dispatch/topics/handler-contract.md) for
191	the return types themselves.
192	
193	## A worked example
194	
195	Every attribute below is exercised by
196	`crates/standout-fixtures/src/derive_surface.rs`, which compiles under
197	`deny(warnings)` against a single `standout` dependency.
198	
199	```rust
200	use clap::{Arg, ArgAction, ArgMatches, Command};
201	use standout::cli::{App, CommandContext, Dispatch, Output};
202	use standout::{handler, EmbeddedTemplates};
203	
204	#[derive(serde::Serialize)]
205	pub struct Units {
206	    pub names: Vec<String>,
207	}
208	
209	pub mod handlers {
210	    use super::*;
211	
212	    #[handler]
213	    pub fn list_units(#[flag] all: bool) -> Result<Output<Units>, anyhow::Error> {
214	        let mut names = vec!["ssh".to_string()];
215	        if all {
216	            names.push("cron".to_string());
217	        }
218	        Ok(Output::Render(Units { names }))
219	    }
220	
221	    #[handler]
222	    pub fn about(#[ctx] _ctx: &CommandContext) -> Result<Output<Units>, anyhow::Error> {
223	        Ok(Output::Render(Units { names: vec!["unitctl".to_string()] }))
224	    }
225	
226	    #[handler]
227	    pub fn reload(#[matches] _matches: &ArgMatches) -> Result<(), anyhow::Error> {
228	        Ok(())
229	    }
230	}
231	
232	#[derive(Dispatch)]
233	#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
234	pub enum Commands {
235	    #[dispatch(pure, default)]
236	    ListUnits,
237	    #[dispatch(pure, name = "about-this")]
238	    About,
239	    #[dispatch(pure, silent)]
240	    Reload,
241	}
242	
243	const TEMPLATES: &[(&str, &str)] = &[
244	    ("list-units", "{{ names | join(', ') }}"),
245	    ("about-this", "{{ names | join(', ') }}"),
246	];
247	
248	/// The clap surface `Commands` is registered against. `Dispatch` connects a
249	/// variant to a handler; declaring the handler's arguments stays clap's job,
250	/// so `list-units` carries the `all` its handler reads.
251	fn command() -> Command {
252	    Command::new("unitctl")
253	        .subcommand(
254	            Command::new("list-units")
255	                .arg(Arg::new("all").long("all").action(ArgAction::SetTrue)),
256	        )
257	        .subcommand(Command::new("about-this"))
258	        .subcommand(Command::new("reload"))
259	}
260	
261	fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
262	    let app: App = App::builder()
263	        .templates(EmbeddedTemplates::new(TEMPLATES, ""))
264	        .commands(Commands::dispatch_config())?
265	        .build()?;
266	    app.verify_command(&command())?;
267	    Ok(())
268	}
269	```
270	
271	`ListUnits` registers the command `list-units`, calls
272	`handlers::list_units__handler`, renders the registry entry `list-units`, and
273	runs on a naked invocation. Its `#[flag] all` parameter reads the clap argument
274	`all` that `command()` declares on that subcommand; `verify_command` is what
275	reports the two drifting apart, instead of leaving it to a `get_flag` panic on
276	the first invocation. `About` registers `about-this` and renders the
277	entry of the same name, because `name` changes the registration path and the
278	convention follows it. `Reload` registers `reload`, calls
279	`handlers::reload__handler` and renders nothing, so it needs no template.
280

  inferred name.

The two are mutually exclusive, and expansion rejects the pair with a message
naming both. Without `pure`, the derive calls the named function directly, so
that function must already have the dispatch signature.

### Every variant attribute

Several `#[dispatch(…)]` attributes may sit on one variant; they merge before
anything reads them.

| Attribute | Form | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | `name = "…"` | Registers the command under this name instead of the variant's kebab-case name. Not empty, no `.`. |
| `handler` | `handler = <path>` | Calls this function instead of the inferred one. Excludes `pure`. |
| `pure` | flag | The handler carries `#[handler]`: append `__handler` to the inferred name. Excludes `handler` and `simple`. |
| `simple` | flag | The handler takes only `&ArgMatches`, with no `&CommandContext`. Excludes `pure`. |
| `nested` | flag | The variant is a subcommand group. Requires a single-field tuple variant wrapping another `Dispatch` enum. |
| `skip` | flag | Registers nothing for this variant. |
| `default` | flag | Runs this command on a naked invocation. At most one variant per enum. |
| `template_name` | `template_name = "…"` | Names the template registry entry instead of using the convention. Excludes `silent`, `binary` and `structured_only`. |
| `silent` | flag | The command renders nothing. Excludes `binary`, `structured_only`, `template_name`. |
| `binary` | flag | The command writes bytes rather than a rendered page. Same exclusions. |
| `structured_only` | flag | The command has output only in the structured modes. Same exclusions. |
| `list_view` | flag | Renders through the framework's built-in `standout/list-view` template, unless `template_name` also appears, and attaches a tabular spec to the handler's `Output::Render`. |
| `item_type` | `item_type = "…"` | Names the `Tabular`-implementing item type `list_view` builds its spec from. |
| `questionnaire` | `questionnaire = <path>` | Resolves this questionnaire type before the handler runs. |
| `pre_dispatch` | `pre_dispatch = <path>` | Runs this hook before the handler. |
| `post_dispatch` | `post_dispatch = <path>` | Runs this hook after the handler, before rendering. |
| `post_output` | `post_output = <path>` | Runs this hook after the output is produced. |
| `pipe_to` | `pipe_to = "…"` | Sends the output to this command and keeps the original. |
| `pipe_through` | `pipe_through = "…"` | Replaces the output with this command's stdout. |
| `pipe_to_clipboard` | flag | Sends the output to the clipboard. |

An unrecognized key fails expansion with a message listing every key above.

### Nested commands

`#[dispatch(nested)]` marks a variant that wraps another `Dispatch` enum:

```rust,ignore
#[derive(Dispatch)]
#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
enum Commands {
    #[dispatch(nested)]
    Pr(PrCommands),
}
```

The derive registers the group rather than a command, and the inner enum's own
variants register beneath it. Registration paths are dot-joined as the
recursion descends, so `pr checks list` registers the path `pr.checks.list`.

### How a command finds its template

With no `template_name` and no absence marker (`silent`, `binary`,
`structured_only`), the template name **is** the registration path with each
`.` replaced by `/`, and **no extension appended**:

| Registration path | Template name |
| --- | --- |
| `list` | `list` |
| `pr.checks.list` | `pr/checks/list` |

The registry then resolves that name against `.jinja`, `.jinja2`, `.j2`,
`.stpl` and `.txt`, in that priority order — so a nested `pr checks list`
command is rendered by `src/templates/pr/checks/list.jinja`. A name may be
looked up with or without an extension; the extension is stripped and the base
name retried.

`#[dispatch(template_name = "…")]` replaces that name with a registry entry you
choose, which is how two commands share one template.

## `#[handler]`

### Parameter attributes

Every typed parameter carries one of four attributes, references included: the
macro reads the value out of `ArgMatches` (or hands over the dispatcher's own
reference) by the attribute, never by the type, so a `&CommandContext` still
needs `#[ctx]` and an `&ArgMatches` still needs `#[matches]`.

| Attribute | Type | Where the value comes from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `#[flag]` | `bool` | `matches.get_flag(id)` |
| `#[arg]` | `T` | a required argument |
| `#[arg]` | `Option<T>` | an optional argument |
| `#[arg]` | `Vec<T>` | a repeated argument |
| `#[ctx]` | `&CommandContext` | the dispatcher |
| `#[matches]` | `&ArgMatches` | the dispatcher, unparsed |

### From a parameter name to a clap argument id

**Underscores become hyphens.** A parameter named `no_legend` reads the
argument whose id is `no-legend`.

Clap's own derive ids an argument by the field name it comes from, so the two
disagree unless one of them says so. Either side can:

```rust,ignore
#[arg(id = "no-legend")]        // on the clap-derive field
no_legend: bool,

#[flag(name = "no_legend")]     // on the handler parameter
no_legend: bool,
```

`app.verify_command(&cmd)` reports the mismatch at build time rather than
leaving it to a runtime `get_flag` panic.

A parameter named with a raw identifier drops the `r#` first, the way clap's
derive drops it from a field name: `r#type` reads the argument id `type`.

### What `#[handler]` generates

For `fn list`, four items:

| Item | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `list` | the original function, unchanged apart from the parameter attributes being removed — still directly callable from a test |
| `list__handler(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext)` | the wrapper that extracts the arguments and calls `list`. It returns **the function's own annotated return type**, verbatim |
| `list__expected_args() -> Vec<ExpectedArg>` | what `verify_command` reads |
| `list_Handler` | a unit struct implementing `Handler` — the registrable item |

The `Result<T, E>` to `Output::Render` wrap happens inside `Handler::handle`,
not inside `list__handler`, and that is what makes the two registration methods
accept different things. `AppBuilder::command_with` takes an `impl Handler`, so
`handlers::list_Handler` works for any of the three return shapes.
`GroupBuilder::command_with` — which is what `#[derive(Dispatch)]` reaches —
takes a closure returning `HandlerResult<T>`, so it accepts
`handlers::list__handler` only when the function was annotated
`-> Result<Output<T>, E>` or `-> Result<(), E>`. The un-suffixed
`handlers::list` is registrable through neither.

See the [handler contract](../crates/dispatch/topics/handler-contract.md) for
the return types themselves.

## A worked example

Every attribute below is exercised by
`crates/standout-fixtures/src/derive_surface.rs`, which compiles under
`deny(warnings)` against a single `standout` dependency.

```rust
use clap::{Arg, ArgAction, ArgMatches, Command};
use standout::cli::{App, CommandContext, Dispatch, Output};
use standout::{handler, EmbeddedTemplates};

#[derive(serde::Serialize)]
pub struct Units {
    pub names: Vec<String>,
}

pub mod handlers {
    use super::*;

    #[handler]
    pub fn list_units(#[flag] all: bool) -> Result<Output<Units>, anyhow::Error> {
        let mut names = vec!["ssh".to_string()];
        if all {
            names.push("cron".to_string());
        }
        Ok(Output::Render(Units { names }))
    }

    #[handler]
    pub fn about(#[ctx] _ctx: &CommandContext) -> Result<Output<Units>, anyhow::Error> {
        Ok(Output::Render(Units { names: vec!["unitctl".to_string()] }))
    }

    #[handler]
    pub fn reload(#[matches] _matches: &ArgMatches) -> Result<(), anyhow::Error> {
        Ok(())
    }
}

#[derive(Dispatch)]
#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
pub enum Commands {
    #[dispatch(pure, default)]
    ListUnits,
    #[dispatch(pure, name = "about-this")]
    About,
    #[dispatch(pure, silent)]
    Reload,
}

const TEMPLATES: &[(&str, &str)] = &[
    ("list-units", "{{ names | join(', ') }}"),
    ("about-this", "{{ names | join(', ') }}"),
];

/// The clap surface `Commands` is registered against. `Dispatch` connects a
/// variant to a handler; declaring the handler's arguments stays clap's job,
/// so `list-units` carries the `all` its handler reads.
fn command() -> Command {
    Command::new("unitctl")
        .subcommand(
            Command::new("list-units")
                .arg(Arg::new("all").long("all").action(ArgAction::SetTrue)),
        )
        .subcommand(Command::new("about-this"))
        .subcommand(Command::new("reload"))
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let app: App = App::builder()
        .templates(EmbeddedTemplates::new(TEMPLATES, ""))
        .commands(Commands::dispatch_config())?
        .build()?;
    app.verify_command(&command())?;
    Ok(())
}
```

`ListUnits` registers the command `list-units`, calls
`handlers::list_units__handler`, renders the registry entry `list-units`, and
runs on a naked invocation. Its `#[flag] all` parameter reads the clap argument
`all` that `command()` declares on that subcommand; `verify_command` is what
reports the two drifting apart, instead of leaving it to a `get_flag` panic on
the first invocation. `About` registers `about-this` and renders the
entry of the same name, because `name` changes the registration path and the
convention follows it. `Reload` registers `reload`, calls
`handlers::reload__handler` and renders nothing, so it needs no template.
